prompt: Match each answer to what the lesson's client does with it.

pairs.right: stops: the server read it and said no
waits as long as Retry-After says
waits, then tries again, not knowing what happened

right_distractors: moves the session to the cache

prompt: Why is a 400 not retried by `retry.ts`?

choices.text: A 400 means the server is overloaded
choices.why: That is 503, or 429.

choices.text: The server deletes the session after a 400, so there is nothing left to send
choices.why: The server saved nothing; the request was refused.

choices.text: The same request gets the same answer
choices.why: Right. The server read it, and nothing has changed.

choices.text: fetch throws on a 400
choices.why: fetch resolves with any status; the code reads it.

prompt: A request gets 401 because the access token expired. What does the lesson say about retrying it?

choices.text: Refresh the token, then send it again
choices.why: Right. Something has to change first, which is why it is not a plain retry.

choices.text: Move it to dead for the person
choices.why: The person can do nothing about an expired token.

choices.text: Drop it, since the person is signed out
choices.why: Expired is not signed out, and dropping it loses the change.

choices.text: Retry it with backoff, like a 503
choices.why: The same token gets the same 401.

prompt: What would happen without `AbortSignal.timeout` on each attempt?

choices.text: The 503s would be treated as successes
choices.why: Statuses are read the same way either way.

choices.text: Node would refuse to send a request that has no deadline attached to it
choices.why: It sends it; there is just no deadline.

choices.text: Every request would be retried twice
choices.why: The timeout does not decide how many tries.

choices.text: A server that never answers would hold the attempt for ever
choices.why: Right. The connection is open and nothing ends the wait.

prompt: What does jitter add to exponential backoff?

choices.text: A limit on the number of tries
choices.why: That is TRIES; jitter is about when.

choices.text: A random point below the ceiling
choices.why: Right. Full jitter picks anywhere from zero to it.

choices.text: A doubling of the wait on each failure
choices.why: The doubling is the exponential part.

choices.text: A wait the server chooses and sends in a header
choices.why: That is Retry-After.

prompt: A server comes back after a minute down. Why does it matter that the phones that failed used jitter?

choices.text: Each phone uses less battery, because the radio wakes fewer times while it is waiting
choices.why: The lesson's point is the server's load.

choices.text: They would all return at once
choices.why: Right. That second outage is the thundering herd.

choices.text: The server can tell the phones apart
choices.why: Jitter changes when they ask, not who they are.

choices.text: Retries with jitter never fail
choices.why: They fail as often; they arrive spread out.

prompt: With BASE 1000 ms and no cap, how many milliseconds is the ceiling on attempt 8?
A colleague proposes `wait = ceiling` with a fixed 500 ms added to every phone, 'so nobody retries instantly'. What does the lesson's schedule predict?

choices.text: The phones spread out, since 500 ms is a delay
choices.why: The same delay for everybody moves the spike, it does not spread it.

choices.text: Fewer requests reach the server
choices.why: The same number arrive; only the timing differs.

choices.text: The cap stops working
choices.why: The cap is unaffected.

choices.text: They still arrive together, half a second later
choices.why: Right. Spreading needs each phone to choose differently.

prompt: After a 429 with `Retry-After: 2`, how long did `retry.ts` wait?

choices.why: Right. The server's number replaced the formula's.

choices.text: 5000 ms, the cap
choices.why: The cap only limits the header's value.

choices.text: 2 ms, the first jittered wait
choices.why: That is what the formula alone chose with seed 7.

choices.text: It did not wait; a 429 is not retried
choices.why: A 429 is retried, more slowly.

prompt: Why does the client keep the cap even when the server sends `Retry-After`?

choices.text: Retry-After is measured in minutes
choices.why: It is seconds, or a date.

choices.text: Because the header is only a suggestion browsers ignore
choices.why: The client honours it, under the cap.

choices.text: So a server's mistake cannot close a phone's outbox for a day
choices.why: Right. The client takes the smaller of the two.

choices.text: The cap makes the server answer faster
choices.why: The cap changes only the client.

prompt: After five 503s, `retry.ts` gives up. Which are true of the operation then? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: it is still in the outbox
choices.why: Giving up is not deleting.

choices.text: the next drain starts it from attempt 1
choices.why: That is what the program prints.

choices.text: it is in the dead table
choices.why: A 503 is not the server's answer about it.

choices.text: the server saved it on the fifth try
choices.why: Every try got a 503.

prompt: The header a server sends with a 429 or a 503 to say how long to wait is ___.
What did the server's `drop` do in the lesson's run?

choices.text: Saved it, then hung up
choices.why: Right. The work was done; the answer was lost.

choices.text: Refused the session with an error
choices.why: It answered nothing.

choices.text: Threw the request away unread, so nothing reached the list of sessions
choices.why: Then there would have been one session, n1 from the retry.

choices.text: Waited two seconds, then answered
choices.why: That is the 429's Retry-After.

prompt: After the `drop` run, how many minutes of guitar does the server hold for 23 October?
Why can the client not tell a lost answer from a request that never arrived?

choices.text: fetch hides the difference on purpose
choices.why: There is no difference for it to show.

choices.text: The server sends the same error code for both
choices.why: In both cases the client receives nothing at all.

choices.text: In both, nothing comes back
choices.why: Right. Silence is all it has.

choices.text: Node keeps no log of requests it sent
choices.why: A log would show it sent one; not whether it arrived.

prompt: A planner never retries a POST, to avoid duplicates. A student creates a session in a lift and the answer is lost. What does the lesson say follows?

choices.text: Nothing bad: the server saved it, so the phone marks it as synced on its own
choices.why: The phone does not know that.

choices.text: It stays pending on the phone, and the server is never asked again
choices.why: Right. Lesson 7's pending, for ever.

choices.text: The server notices and sends the answer later
choices.why: HTTP has no way for it to do that.

choices.text: The session is moved to dead
choices.why: Dead is for a 4xx, and there was no answer.

prompt: Put in order what happened in the `drop` run.
items: the client sends the first POST
the server saves n1 and closes the connection
the client sees no answer and waits
the second POST is saved as n2 and its 201 arrives

prompt: Which change would let the server recognise the second POST in the `drop` run as the same operation?

choices.text: A longer timeout on the client
choices.why: The answer was not slow; it was never sent.

choices.text: Comparing the body with the last session saved
choices.why: A second identical session the person meant to add would be refused.

choices.text: Jitter on the retry
choices.why: Jitter changes when, not what the server can recognise.

choices.text: An identity the client chooses before the first try and sends with every retry
choices.why: Right. That is lesson 10's idempotency key.
